metadata.title: The influence of ICT competencies on English digital reading achievement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata restricted to students who completed the digital reading assessment in English in Macau, Hong Kong, and Singapore (total n=7703). The methodology describes multiple imputation for missing data and hierarchical regression models, but it does not report the use of PISA complex-sample weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the analysis is regression-based (not ML algorithms that would typically require weight-aware training), the manuscript’s omission of weighting details makes it unclear whether estimates are population-representative for each economy. Analysts using the PISA international database should apply the appropriate student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) consistent with PISA technical documentation, especially given the clustered school sampling design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 digital reading data in English. From the full PISA 2018 dataset, selected students who adopted English as the test language in Macau, Hong Kong, and Singapore (n=7703). The dependent variable was PV1READ (plausible value PV1READ) for English digital reading achievement; missing values were handled via MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS 26.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) English digital reading (PV1READ) — Macau, Hong Kong, Singapore
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical regression (standardized betas). Model R²: Macau 0.162 (Model 1) → 0.298 (Model 2) → 0.299 (Model 4) → 0.212 (Model 5) → 0.256 (Model 9); Hong Kong 0.271 → 0.298 → 0.299 → 0.275 → 0.320; Singapore 0.149 → 0.164 → 0.164 → 0.158 → 0.208. Key betas (Model 9): Macau SES β=0.282***, Gender β=-0.169***, Interest in ICT β=0.254***, ICT as social interaction topic β=-0.196***; Hong Kong SES β=0.428***, Gender β=-0.164***, Interest in ICT β=0.060 (ns), ICT as social interaction topic β=-0.210***; Singapore SES β=0.348***, Gender β=-0.050* , Interest in ICT β=0.118***, ICT as social interaction topic β=-0.249***.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 English digital reading data (PV1READ) for students in Macau, Hong Kong, and Singapore, the study leveraged socioeconomic status (SES), gender, ICT use during lessons, ICT use outside lessons, and interest in ICT to explain English digital reading achievement, finding that SES was consistently positively associated while gender was negatively associated, and that ICT literacy (especially ICT use outside lessons) showed limited or negative contributions whereas ICT attitudes (interest, autonomy, competence) were generally positive and ICT as a social-interaction topic was negative. This indicates that improving students’ ICT-related learning attitudes and regulating off-task ICT use may support English digital reading achievement, though the study’s hierarchical regression design and single-PV outcome (PV1READ) limit causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 digital reading achievement in English using PV1READ for 7703 15-year-old students from Macau (n=679), Hong Kong (n=348), and Singapore (n=6676). Missing data were addressed with MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS 26, and the authors estimate hierarchical regression models with gender and SES as controls, then add ICT literacy (ICT use during lessons; ICT use outside lessons) and ICT attitudes (interest, autonomy, competence, and ICT as a social-interaction topic). Across economies, SES shows a positive association with English digital reading achievement, while gender shows a negative association. ICT literacy effects are small and often negative (notably ICT use outside lessons in Macau), whereas interest, autonomy, and competence are positive predictors; ICT as a topic in social interaction is negative in all three economies. Limitations include the use of a single plausible value (PV1READ) and the absence of reported survey-weighting/replicate-weight procedures, so results may not fully reflect PISA’s complex sampling design.
